opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's a really interesting relationship right now, and a somewhat unusual one compared to other areas of machine learning.

On the industry side, the big labs have two things academia mostly doesn't: access to frontier models, including their weights and training details, and enormous compute. If you want to study how a truly state-of-the-art model represents something, or train sparse autoencoders at scale on a huge model, that's very hard to do from a university. So a lot of the headline interpretability results come out of industry, and that's natural.

But I don't think that makes academia less important. In some ways it frees us to do different kinds of work. Academics can be more skeptical and more methodological. We can ask: does this technique actually do what we claim? Are our evaluations meaningful? Is a feature in a dictionary really the model's own variable, or an artifact of the method? A lot of my interest is in causal approaches, like interventions on representations, and that kind of careful benchmarking and stress-testing is something academia is well positioned to do because we're not tied to one company's agenda or product timeline.

Open-weight models have also changed things a lot. Once there are capable open models, academics can do serious interpretability work without being inside a lab, and that's helped the field grow very quickly. Open-source tooling matters too. Shared libraries for interventions and analysis lower the barrier for everyone.

There's also a lot of movement between the two worlds. Many students intern at labs, people go back and forth, and ideas flow both ways. Industry often picks up methods that started in academic papers and scales them, and academics then probe what those scaled-up results really mean. I think that's healthy.

The main tension I'd point to is openness. Interpretability is partly a safety and scientific-understanding project, and that works best when results, methods, and ideally artifacts are shared so others can reproduce and challenge them. Labs have commercial and safety reasons not to share everything, and that's understandable, but the field benefits a lot when they do publish openly. So my hope is for an ecosystem where industry provides scale and access, academia provides rigor and independent scrutiny, and both are fairly open with each other.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of it as a pretty healthy division of labor right now, with some real tension underneath it.

The industry labs have the thing academia can't get: the models themselves, at frontier scale, with full access to weights and activations and the training data. If you want to study how a frontier model represents something, you basically have to be inside a lab. That's where a lot of the headline results have come from, like the sparse autoencoder work and the circuit-tracing work.

What academia has is time and freedom. You can spend two years on a question that doesn't need to ship, and you can be skeptical in a way that's harder when your employer has a product riding on the answer. A lot of the methodological critique in interpretability has come from academic groups, people asking whether a feature is actually causally doing what the dashboard says it's doing, or whether a method generalizes beyond the handful of examples in the paper. That kind of adversarial check is really important, and I don't think the field should outsource it to the labs that built the methods.

The tension is that the access gap keeps growing. Open models help a lot, and I'd say most academic interp work now runs on Llama- or Gemma-class models, which is fine for a lot of questions. But if the interesting behavior only shows up at a scale you can't run on a university cluster, you're studying the wrong object. So I spend a lot of time thinking about which questions are scale-invariant enough that an academic can actually answer them.

The other thing I'd say is that the two sides talk more than people assume. A lot of grad students intern at labs, a lot of lab researchers came out of academic groups and still publish openly. The flow of people and ideas is pretty porous. Where it breaks down is incentives, not culture. Labs are increasingly pulled toward interpretability that's useful for safety or for the product, and academics are pulled toward what's publishable. Both are legitimate, but neither one by itself is going to produce the kind of foundational understanding I think we actually need. So I'd like to see more of the middle: academics with real compute and model access, and labs willing to fund slow work that doesn't pay off next quarter.

astra-6.text:
I think they play complementary roles. Industry has access to the models, the compute, and the practical problems that make interpretability useful. If you’re trying to understand why a deployed model behaves a certain way, it helps enormously to be close to the people building and using it.

Academia has more room to step back and ask foundational questions: What do we mean by an explanation? How do we know that an interpretability method actually captures what the model is doing? Those questions can be difficult to prioritize when you’re working toward a product deadline.

The relationship works best when there’s a feedback loop. Practical problems can inform academic research, and academic work can give industry better ways to assess whether its explanations are reliable. But that requires enough access for researchers outside a company to test claims independently. Otherwise, you risk having a field where only the people building the systems can meaningfully study them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Academia gives researchers room to step back and ask foundational questions: What would it mean to understand a model? How do we know an explanation is faithful, rather than just plausible? Industry brings access to the models, compute, and practical problems that can help test those ideas.

The tension is that their incentives differ. An academic project might aim for a clean result on a small model, while an industry team needs something useful for a much larger system. Neither automatically translates into the other.

So I’d like to see a tighter feedback loop: practical failures motivating academic questions, and academic methods being tested against realistic problems. Access matters a lot here. If only people inside a handful of companies can study the most capable models, it becomes harder for the broader research community to independently check what we think we understand.
